title: The best gift (351–359)
hookLine: the gift of the dhamma beats all gifts; its taste beats all tastes (Dhammapada 354)
last: JĀLA — STEP OUT OF THE WEB.

cards: Some of the gifts that last aren't things at all. They're sentences someone said at the right moment. A teacher who told you that you were good at something.
A grandparent who showed you how to do a thing with your hands. A friend who said, you don't have to carry this alone. The object wears out; the sentence doesn't.
The commentary says today's verse answered a question the gods themselves were arguing about.

teach.b: In the heaven of the thirty-three gods, the commentary says, the devas got into a debate. Which gift is best? Which taste is best?
Which delight is best? No one could settle it, so Sakka, their king, came down to ask the Buddha.

teach.h: THE GIFT OF THE DHAMMA EXCEEDS ALL.
teach.b: The answer is verse three hundred fifty-four, in Max Müller's English: "The gift of the law exceeds all gifts; the sweetness of the law exceeds all sweetness; the delight in the law exceeds all delights; the extinction of thirst overcomes all pain."
Where Müller says the law, the Pali says dhamma: the teaching, the way things truly are. So the best gift is the teaching.
Buddhist tradition calls it dhamma-dana, the gift of dhamma, and says it outshines even gifts of food and robes, which are themselves honored.

teach.h: THE END OF THIRST ENDS ALL PAIN.
teach.b: The last line ties the whole chapter together: the end of thirst, of tanha, ends all pain. The creeper, the root, the web all come undone. The chapter's other verses circle the same place.
Tradition places one soon after his awakening, as the Buddha's reply when a wandering ascetic asked who his teacher was: I have conquered all, I know all, and I have no teacher.
Another says riches ruin the foolish, but not those who seek the far shore.

And the chapter closes with fields: fields are spoiled by weeds, and people are spoiled by passion, hatred, delusion and lust. Gifts given to those free of these weeds, the verses say, bring great reward.
The verse doesn't keep the gift of the dhamma for monks. One true teaching, passed on at the right moment, is a small share of it.

how: Many Buddhists sponsor the printing of dhamma books to give away, and teachers describe the gift of the dhamma (dhamma-dana) as the highest gift; lay people often dedicate the merit of giving to others.

o: the gift of the teaching, the best gift of all
a donation of food and robes to the monks
money given to build a temple or shrine

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: king of the gods, brought the question

s: the Pali says dhamma: the teaching, the way things are.
the tradition says gifts of food and robes are worthless
they are honored; the gift of the dhamma is said to outshine them.
the commentary says gods argued over which gift is best
Sakka, their king, brought the question to the Buddha.

games.q: you're Sakka, king of the gods. your court can't agree on which gift, taste and delight is best. what do you do?
o: decide it yourself by royal order.
go down and ask the Buddha.
games.why: the commentary says Sakka asked the Buddha, who answered with verse 354: the gift of the dhamma exceeds all gifts.

practice: Think back over the last few weeks of verses, the forest, the bigger joy, the elephant bearing the arrow, the creeper, the web, and pick one line that has stayed with you.
Think of one person who might need that line right now, and hold the two together, the verse and the person, wishing them well. Then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Dhammadāna. The gift of the dhamma, the teaching: it exceeds all gifts, and the end of thirst ends all pain.

orig.note: Pali dhammadāna: the gift of the dhamma; verse 354 calls it the gift that exceeds all gifts.
